posts.title: Amethyst 1.21 brings NApplets into notes and simplifies Web of Trust setup
posts.description: Amethyst v1.21.0 runs NApplets and WebXDC apps inside notes, adds listening and game formats, and introduces a guided Web of Trust setup with explicit security limits.
posts.excerpt: The client can now open small Nostr apps inside a note and guide eligible accounts through trust-provider setup, while tightening what embedded code may access.
posts.content:
[Amethyst v1.21.0](https://github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/releases/tag/v1.21.0), published on 1 November 2026, can run NApplets and WebXDC apps inside the notes that carry them. It also adds a Web of Trust setup card, drss.io listening, Pico-8 cartridges and more kinds of content to Home. This is a released update to an existing client, not a new client launch.

The useful change is not just another media renderer. A note can now be an entry point to a small application while the host client remains responsible for storage, network access, signing and decryption. That makes the permission boundary part of the user experience.

## Apps inside notes

On Android 11 or newer and on desktop, a NApplet can show a Run here action. It stays inside the note with controls to open or stop it. If an action would require a prompt, the feed refuses it and offers to open the app separately instead.

WebXDC attachments run in separate storage for each account and app, with no network, WebRTC or key access. Amethyst also adds interfaces for files chosen through the operating system, Blossom uploads, common Nostr actions and handing a task to another NApplet. These are permissions exposed by the host, not direct access to an account secret.

Desktop builds now bundle Chromium for NApplets and nSites. The tagged changelog also says older aggregate manifests must be republished for the current single-artifact format. A signed old package does not automatically become compatible with the new host rules.

## A guided Web of Trust entry point

Accounts that follow at least ten people and do not have a trust provider can see a Web of Trust card on Home. Before sign-up, Amethyst sends the profile, follows, mutes and relay list to the selected provider. It then adopts the provider relay for trusted, search, indexer and favorite roles and moves Global feeds to it.

That is a convenient setup path, but it is also a data and routing decision. The provider remains visible to the user, and the card says initial scores may take about ten minutes. The release notes do not establish that every provider uses the same scoring model or privacy policy.

## Hardening after a security review

The release narrows what embedded code can do. Reading encrypted direct messages, gift wraps or private lists requires a separate decrypt grant. Only events with valid signatures reach an app. Cookies and WebRTC are removed from every embedded frame, local-network and DNS leaks are closed, and site-card prefetching is limited to public HTTPS servers within a shared budget.

These are published hardening changes, not evidence of an exploited incident. The upstream changelog does not cite a CVE or say that an attack was observed. This review inspected tagged source and release evidence; it did not execute third-party NApplets, inspect a trust provider or test Android and desktop behavior.

## What else changed

The same release can play Pico-8 cartridges, read drss.io shows and listening progress, display more Home content types, and offer a chess feed in release builds. Those additions make Amethyst a broader host, which is why the capability boundary deserves as much attention as the feature list.

For builders, the main discovery is a client architecture that treats small apps as untrusted guests. For users, the practical question is narrower: which provider or embedded app receives which data, and whether the requested capability matches the task.

posts.title: Nostr WoT SDK stabilizes passkey recovery and provider signing
posts.description: Stable npm packages now expose explicit passkey modes, encrypted recovery records and a provider signer with strict origin and account checks.
posts.excerpt: The stable SDK release separates derived and stored passkeys, preserves recovery choices and adds provider signing without guessing an account mode.
posts.seoDescription: Nostr WoT SDK publishes stable passkey recovery packages with explicit key modes, encrypted vault records and pinned provider signing.

sources.title: Support Nosskey account recovery and provider signing

posts.content:
The Nostr WoT SDK passkey work is now on stable npm tags. The npm registry lists [`@nostr-wot/identity` 1.1.0](https://registry.npmjs.org/@nostr-wot%2Fidentity) and [`nostr-wot-sdk` 3.0.1](https://registry.npmjs.org/nostr-wot-sdk) as `latest`, both published on 23 October 2026 from the commit that merged the [stable release pull request](https://github.com/nostr-wot/nostr-wot-sdk/pull/23). The package source is unchanged from the tested release candidates.

This release is for developers building signers and Nostr applications. It makes passkey identity modes explicit, adds encrypted recovery records that can move through several host-controlled storage paths and supports an independently implemented provider signer for existing Nosskey accounts.

## Derived and stored passkeys are different systems

The identity package treats a passkey in one of two modes. A derived passkey deterministically produces the Nostr private key from WebAuthn PRF output. A stored passkey protects an existing private key, seed or multi-account vault encrypted under that output.

New credentials carry a tagged user handle that identifies the mode before storage is read. A stored credential is never silently interpreted as derived. When an older untagged credential does not provide enough evidence, `resolvePasskeyIdentity` returns `ambiguous` with a public-key candidate instead of guessing. The application must show that key and obtain confirmation before deriving a secret.

The distinction protects identity continuity. Derived mode ties the identity to the passkey calculation. Stored mode lets the same identity be protected again under another relying party, provided the host imports and re-encrypts it deliberately.

## Recovery stays under host control

[`@nostr-wot/identity/vault`](https://github.com/nostr-wot/nostr-wot-sdk/blob/384023f947e7dcfe4d54f7862308cdf78040067c/docs/passkey-recovery.md) supplies portable cryptography, record validation and orchestration. It does not call authenticators or open relay connections itself. The host provides WebAuthn or native credential operations, relay transport, event signing, signature verification and the user interface around consent.

Stored records can contain one key or a vault with several accounts. The encrypted record binds its type, relying-party ID, author and credential ID as authenticated data. A provider write must first inspect existing storage. Any nonempty blob requires explicit overwrite confirmation, including when the old data cannot be decoded. A refused or failed provider write is an error and is not silently redirected to relays.

Relay recovery is also explicit. The host must allow it, name the relays and receive at least one acknowledgement. New records use provisional kind `31778`, which is not reserved by an upstream NIP. Existing legacy records remain readable. A local largeBlob write, a relay acknowledgement or a provider claim each proves only that operation, not that another device can recover the account.

## Existing Nosskey accounts get two integration paths

[`nostr-wot-sdk` 3.0.1](https://github.com/nostr-wot/nostr-wot-sdk/pull/22) can read explicit Nosskey backups in direct-key or NIP-44 wrapped-key form while preserving their original PRF inputs. The recovered public key is checked against the backup, and the reader does not fall back between modes when evidence is missing.

Applications that do not want to import a private key can use `NosskeyIframeSigner`. It pins the iframe window, HTTPS origin and selected account, verifies returned event content and signatures, applies request timeouts and requires explicit teardown. Provider consent and browser iframe or WebAuthn support are still external requirements. Protocol compatibility alone does not establish availability on every device or browser.

## What changes for implementers

Install the stable packages rather than the `next` candidates:

```bash
npm install @nostr-wot/identity@1.1.0 nostr-wot-sdk@3.0.1 nostr-tools
```

Hosts still need device-level tests for their authenticators and provider synchronization. They need to preserve unknown vault fields when rewriting a record, clear returned secret buffers, confirm the public key during migration and show whether recovery data is local, provider-backed or relay-backed. Recovery records are snapshots, so applications also need a policy for refreshing them after account changes.

The stable tags make the tested APIs installable without a prerelease selector. They do not turn passkeys into a universal backup layer. Relying-party authorization remains a trust decision, provisional relay records may evolve, and every application remains responsible for consent, storage durability and a recovery path that users can verify.

posts.title: Nostr WoT 0.8.13 adds passkey recovery and event archives
posts.description: Version 0.8.13 is live in Chrome and Firefox with passkey-protected vault recovery, a full event archive view and stricter NWC payment handling.
posts.excerpt: The extension can now protect and restore a vault with compatible passkeys, inspect archived events in a full tab and preserve uncertain NWC payments from automatic retry.
posts.seoDescription: Nostr WoT 0.8.13 reaches Chrome and Firefox with passkey vault recovery, an event archive explorer, faster startup and safer NWC payment retries.

sources.title: Nostr WoT Extension on Chrome Web Store
Nostr WoT Extension on Firefox Add-ons

posts.content:
[Nostr WoT extension 0.8.13](https://github.com/nostr-wot/nostr-wot-extension/releases/tag/v0.8.13) is available in both supported browser stores. The [Chrome listing](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/nostr-wot-extension/gfmefgdkmjpjinecjchlangpamhclhdo) and [Firefox listing](https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/nostr-wot-extension/) each show version `0.8.13`, updated on 17 October 2026. The release adds passkey-protected vault creation and recovery, a larger event archive interface, popup reliability work and stricter handling of uncertain Lightning payments.

## A passkey can protect and recover the vault

Version 0.8.13 can create or unlock a vault with a compatible passkey. The provider must support discoverable credentials, user verification and the WebAuthn PRF extension. Password and seed-based setup remain available when that path is not suitable.

Recovery is not reduced to one provider. The extension can save an encrypted full-vault snapshot in supported provider storage, create an encrypted recovery file and publish a narrower recovery snapshot to explicitly selected relays. Relay publication remains a separate user action. When provider storage succeeds during setup, the flow moves directly to protection preferences; file and relay alternatives remain available from Passkey settings.

The distinction matters. A provider reporting storage support does not prove that another device has synchronized the blob. A relay returning a signed recovery event does not prove that the snapshot is current or will remain available. The interface therefore separates recorded acknowledgements, availability checks and actual recovery.

Passkeys also stay bound to their relying party. Advanced recovery can use an authorized original domain and then add a new credential for `passkeys.nostrwot.com`, but this is not universal passkey transfer between unrelated applications.

## The archive moves into a full browser tab

The release expands Account Archive from background storage and import tools into a full event explorer. It can switch accounts, show bounded search and paginated results, group public chats and encrypted messages, and reveal supported private content only when requested. Profile, contact and relay-list views show their latest stored versions and update dates.

Deleting a selected local record removes it from the local archive. It does not publish a Nostr deletion request and does not claim that relays erased the original event. External profile images and banners may still load from their source URLs, which is a separate privacy consideration from decrypting message content locally.

## Payment safeguards treat uncertainty as uncertainty

For wallet providers that return a fee quote, the extension reserves the invoice amount plus the quoted fee against the rolling 24-hour silent-payment allowance. A later quote cannot exceed the reservation or the configured fee policy without another approval.

Nostr Wallet Connect does not provide an enforceable fee-limit capability. Its silent-payment budget therefore remains invoice-only, and an explicit fee ceiling is refused instead of being presented as enforced. If a relay rejects a request after payment dispatch, the result stays unknown and the extension does not automatically retry it. A relay acknowledgement alone cannot establish whether the wallet paid.

## Availability is channel-specific

The public stores establish availability for Chrome and Firefox at version `0.8.13`. The GitHub release also provides separate Chrome and Firefox ZIP files, source and checksums. Those facts do not establish a Safari release or support from every passkey provider.

The practical change is a broader recovery boundary, not the removal of recovery responsibility. Users still need to verify that their provider supports the required passkey features, retain an appropriate fallback and test that the recovered public key matches the intended account.

posts.title: Mostro 0.20 defers payouts and publishes node health
posts.description: Mostro v0.20.0 adds LND sync monitoring, payment deferral and signed health events, with limits that clients and operators need to understand.
posts.excerpt: A node can still announce itself while payouts fail. Mostro adds separate health signals and automatic controls for an unsynced Lightning backend.

sources.title: LND sync and payment deferral PR #1065

posts.content:
A node appearing on Nostr does not prove that it can pay. [Mostro v0.20.0](https://github.com/MostroP2P/mostro/releases/tag/v0.20.0), published on 15 October 2026, adds separate health reporting and controls for a Lightning backend that has fallen out of sync. It is an update to an existing exchange daemon, not a new exchange launch.

Mostro carries peer-to-peer trading messages over Nostr and coordinates Lightning payments. Its [release README](https://github.com/MostroP2P/mostro/blob/v0.20.0/README.md) distinguishes the daemon from the clients that people use to trade. That distinction matters here: the new controls run at the node, while clients and monitoring tools must decide how to interpret its reports.

## Why an announcement was not enough

The project's [health documentation](https://github.com/MostroP2P/mostro/blob/v0.20.0/docs/HEALTH.md) describes a 14 October operational failure. LND stopped following the chain, outgoing payments failed and new trades could still open. The ordinary information event continued to appear, so its presence did not expose the payout problem.

The lesson is narrower than a general security claim. Announcing configuration or answering a relay is not the same as completing the payment path. Version 0.20.0 separates those questions rather than treating one as evidence of the other.

## Wait before blaming the buyer

[Pull request #1065](https://github.com/MostroP2P/mostro/pull/1065) adds an LND monitor that polls every 15 seconds. After a sustained 60-second period of unsynced or unreachable LND, outgoing payments wait instead of repeatedly consuming the buyer's payment attempts. Startup also checks the backend before payment jobs begin.

Automatic maintenance has a different threshold. By default, 600 seconds of reported chain desynchronization stops new orders and takes. Recovery requires 300 seconds of stable synchronization before the daemon clears its own automatic maintenance. An operator's separate maintenance decision is not automatically removed.

Unreachable is not identical to unsynced. A backend that does not answer produces an `unknown` check rather than proof of chain desynchronization. Payments can still be deferred without that condition alone enabling automatic maintenance. These distinctions prevent a single green or red label from standing in for several different states.

## A separate report for watchers

[Pull request #1066](https://github.com/MostroP2P/mostro/pull/1066) introduces addressable `kind 38389` health events. The normal publication interval is 60 seconds, with earlier reports when relevant states change. Public tags describe checks such as LND synchronization, payouts, relays and the database, together with an overall status.

Detailed operational metrics can be encrypted with NIP-44 for a configured watchdog public key. Without that configuration, the detailed content is empty. The event does not turn all internal metrics into a public dashboard.

Freshness is part of the design. Reports carry sequence and expiration information. A reader that has no usable health report must not treat its absence as `ok`. Existing clients that do not understand the new event do not gain monitoring merely because the daemon was upgraded.

## What the controls cannot establish

The tagged health documentation explicitly warns that a node reports what its own backend knows. A stale backend may not recognize its own stale view. Comparing the advertised block height with an independent reference remains useful; a signed report identifies its author, not the truth of every operational claim.

The release provides downloadable binaries, source and signed-manifest files. Their presence establishes availability, not successful installation on a particular node. The upstream PRs describe automated coverage and a local Cashu-mode check, but also identify gaps in manual Lightning testing. This source-based review did not run a trading node or send payments.

For builders, the useful discovery is the interface: distinguish identity and configuration announcements from fresh operational health, preserve `unknown` as a real state, and do not turn a backend failure into a buyer's exhausted retry allowance.

posts.title: Amethyst 1.18 adds NIP-85 trust filtering and a new desktop app
posts.description: Amethyst 1.18.0 adds a local NIP-85 trust index for DMs and notifications, and ships shared desktop builds for Linux, macOS and Windows.
posts.excerpt: A provider-supplied trust network can now separate known contacts from new requests without a relay query for every profile.
posts.content:
[Amethyst 1.18.0](https://github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/releases/tag/v1.18.0) was published on 11 October 2026. The release adds a local Web of Trust index based on NIP-85, uses it in direct messages and notifications, and replaces the old desktop interface with the same application shell used on Android.

The release page provides Android packages plus desktop files for Linux on x86-64 and ARM64, Windows on x86-64 and ARM64, and Apple Silicon Macs. The `amy` and `geode` command-line tools also have packages for the three desktop operating systems.

## A trust network that stays local after syncing

[NIP-85](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/85.md) defines signed Trusted Assertion events. For people, kind `30382` identifies the subject in its `d` tag and can carry a `rank` from 0 to 100. A separate kind `10040` event lets a user name the provider and relay they want for each assertion type.

[PR #4375](https://github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/pull/4375) adds the consumer side of that model to Amethyst. The client downloads the selected provider's kind `30382` cards, verifies their signatures and builds a compact local index. Later checks read that index instead of opening a relay subscription for every profile.

The visible effects are broader than a badge. Amethyst can use the selected minimum score when it separates direct messages into **Known** and **New Requests**, filters the **Curated** notification view, collapses replies from outside the network and marks profiles that pass the threshold. The settings screen exposes the provider, minimum score and sync progress. The `amy` command-line client gets matching `trust setup`, `sync`, `status` and `check` commands.

The first provider offered by the onboarding flow is Brainstorm, but the design is not tied to one scoring service. NIP-85 puts provider selection in the user's kind `10040` event, and the Amethyst settings allow that choice and threshold to change.

## The index has a cost and a trust boundary

The pull request reports a measured cold download of about 93 MB for roughly 155,000 cards, completed in 34 seconds in its test setup. That is a project measurement, not a guarantee for every relay or device. On Android, the background worker runs daily only on an unmetered connection with sufficient battery. Opening the app can also start a due sync. Full checks use NIP-77 negentropy, while smaller updates request the newer cards.

This system does not make a score objective. NIP-85 explicitly allows providers to use different algorithms and points of view. A client verifies that an assertion was signed by the chosen provider, not that the provider's ranking is correct. Selecting a provider therefore delegates part of message and notification filtering to that provider's view. Users who dislike the result can change the provider or threshold, and filtering remains off until a provider and a complete network are available.

The local index reduces repeated network queries and makes lookups fast, but it also stores a large derived view of the network on the device. The implementation keeps provider identity and sync state in the index header so that changing providers triggers the appropriate rebuild.

## One interface reaches the desktop

[PR #4372](https://github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/pull/4372) makes the shared `AmethystApp` the default desktop application. Login, account switching, feeds, messages, uploads, scheduled posts and several media features now use the same shared screens as Android. The desktop build also adds native file pickers, operating-system notifications, platform themes and video playback controls.

The pull request records a Linux test in an Ubuntu 24.04 container. It does not claim a hardware test on macOS or Windows, and it lists HLS playback on Linux with GStreamer 1.24 or newer as a known limitation. The release assets also include only ARM64 for macOS, while Linux and Windows cover both ARM64 and x86-64.

Amethyst 1.18 is therefore two changes of different kinds. The desktop work widens where the client runs. The NIP-85 index changes how the client can decide which people and events deserve attention. The latter remains a configurable filter supplied by a chosen third party, not a universal reputation score.

posts.title: Verify NIP-57 zap receipts before counting them
posts.description: A NIP-57 zap receipt is a signed claim from the recipient's LNURL server. Verify its signer, request, invoice, amount and target before counting it.
posts.excerpt: A kind 9735 event is not enough to prove a Lightning payment. Its signature and every binding between the LNURL server, zap request, invoice, amount and target must agree.
posts.seoDescription: Learn how to validate NIP-57 kind 9735 zap receipts, embedded requests, LNURL signer, BOLT11 amount, description hash, targets and proof limits.

sources.title: NIP-57: Lightning Zaps at commit a79e21d
NIP-01: Basic protocol flow at commit a79e21d

posts.content:
A Nostr zap normally leaves a kind `9735` event called a zap receipt. It is useful evidence, but its event kind alone proves almost nothing. A client that counts every `9735` event can accept a forged signer, a changed amount, a different recipient or a receipt copied from another target.

[NIP-57 defines a chain of linked data](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/a79e21d90fce5465b50ef385dd368bba99ec4a0b/57.md): a signed kind `9734` zap request, an LNURL-pay response, a BOLT11 invoice and a signed kind `9735` receipt. Validation means checking every link. Even then, the result is the recipient's LNURL server making a signed statement, not trustless proof that Lightning settled.

## Start with a valid Nostr event

First validate the receipt as a normal Nostr event under NIP-01. Recompute its event ID from the canonical serialization and verify its Schnorr signature against `pubkey`. Reject malformed tags and confirm that `kind` is exactly `9735`.

Relay copies of the same event keep the same ID. Deduplicate by event ID before doing any totals, otherwise the same receipt found on several relays can be counted several times.

The receipt should have empty `content`. Its useful data is in tags:

- `bolt11` carries the Lightning invoice;
- `description` carries the JSON-encoded kind `9734` zap request;
- `p` identifies the recipient;
- optional `e` or `a` tags identify the event or addressable event being zapped;
- optional `P` identifies the sender when the request included one.

## Bind the signer to the recipient's LNURL service

The receipt's public key must equal the `nostrPubkey` returned by the recipient's LNURL-pay endpoint. A valid Nostr signature from any other key is not a valid receipt for that payment flow.

This check has a time boundary. LNURL configuration can change, so software that needs an audit trail should retain the LNURL metadata used when the invoice was requested. A later lookup can show the current server key, but it may not reconstruct the key that was authorized at payment time.

## Validate the embedded zap request

Parse the `description` tag as the original kind `9734` event. Then verify its ID and signature like any other signed event. NIP-57 also requires a structurally valid request: exactly one `p` tag, no more than one `e`, `a` or `P` tag, and a `relays` tag with relay URLs where the receipt can be published.

Compare the request with the receipt. The receipt must copy the request's `p` tag and any `e`, `a` and `P` tags. If a receipt points at a different recipient or target, do not count it for the page, profile or event currently being displayed.

If the request contains an `lnurl` tag, NIP-57 says it should match the recipient's LNURL. Treat a mismatch as failed binding rather than harmless metadata drift.

## Make the invoice and amount agree

Decode the `bolt11` invoice rather than trusting a displayed amount. When the zap request has an `amount` tag, the invoice amount must equal it. The LNURL callback request must also have used that same amount.

The BOLT11 invoice's description hash should equal the SHA-256 hash of the exact JSON string in the receipt's `description` tag. This prevents a valid invoice from being attached to a different zap request after the fact. Hash the bytes exactly as carried; parsing and reserializing JSON can change whitespace or key order and produce a different hash.

A receipt may also contain a `preimage` tag. Its hash can be compared with the invoice payment hash, but NIP-57 warns that this is not meaningful independent proof because the recipient created the invoice and already knows the preimage after settlement.

## Know what a valid receipt does not prove

After all checks pass, the receipt establishes internal consistency and an authorized server signature. It does not provide cryptographic proof to an outside observer that the invoice was actually paid. NIP-57 explicitly says the receipt author can lie.

That limitation should shape the interface. “Receipt verified” can mean the event, signer, request, invoice, amount and target agree. It should not be presented as trustless settlement proof. For accounting, rewards or access control, use independent Lightning settlement data controlled by the party making the decision.

## A practical validation order

Use a fixed order so failures are understandable:

1. Verify the kind `9735` event ID and signature.
2. Deduplicate identical receipt event IDs across relays.
3. Confirm the signer matches the LNURL `nostrPubkey` used for the invoice.
4. Parse and verify the embedded kind `9734` request.
5. Compare `p`, `e`, `a`, `P` and optional `lnurl` bindings.
6. Decode BOLT11 and compare its amount with the request amount.
7. Compare the invoice description hash with the exact `description` string.
8. Report the result as a signed server claim, not independent payment proof.

This sequence turns a convenient social signal into something a client can explain and debug. It also keeps the final limitation visible: NIP-57 can authenticate who issued a consistent receipt, but it cannot make the issuer unable to lie.

posts.title: Verify NIP-05 without turning a domain into trust
posts.description: NIP-05 confirms a live mapping between a signed Nostr profile, an internet identifier and a domain response. It does not certify the person behind the key.
posts.excerpt: A valid NIP-05 identifier is a two-sided mapping checked at a point in time. Keep the public key as the identity anchor and treat the domain as current evidence, not permanent trust.
posts.seoDescription: Learn the correct NIP-05 verification flow, reverse lookup, lowercase key rules, redirect and CORS checks, caching, relay hints and trust limits.

sources.title: NIP-05: Mapping Nostr keys to DNS-based internet identifiers at commit a79e21d
NIP-01: Basic protocol flow at commit a79e21d

posts.content:
NIP-05 makes a long Nostr public key easier to exchange by linking it to an internet identifier such as `alice@example.com`. The result can help with discovery, but the word “verified” often encourages a stronger conclusion than the protocol supports.

A correct check proves something narrower: the latest signed kind `0` metadata event names an identifier, and the domain currently maps that same name back to the same public key. It does not prove a legal identity, good judgment or trustworthiness. [NIP-05 says explicitly that the mechanism is for identification, not general verification](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/a79e21d90fce5465b50ef385dd368bba99ec4a0b/05.md).

## Start with the signed profile

The forward flow begins with the newest valid kind `0` event for a public key. Its JSON content may contain a `nip05` field:

```json
{
  "name": "Alice",
  "nip05": "alice@example.com"
}
```

Split the value into the local part and domain. The local part is deliberately restricted to lowercase `a-z`, digits and `-_.`. Fetch:

```text
https://example.com/.well-known/nostr.json?name=alice
```

The response must contain a `names` object whose exact `alice` entry is the same 64-character lowercase hexadecimal public key as the kind `0` event. An `npub` value is for display and is not valid in this response.

This comparison is two-sided. The signed profile says “this key claims this identifier.” The HTTPS response says “this domain currently assigns this name to this key.” Display the identifier only when both statements agree.

## Reverse lookup needs the second half too

Search can begin from `alice@example.com`, but it should not stop after the domain returns a key. A client should fetch the returned key’s newest valid kind `0` event and confirm that its `nip05` field contains the same identifier.

Without that reverse check, a domain operator could list any public key that never claimed the address. With it, the lookup demonstrates current agreement between the key holder and the domain operator.

The special local part `_` may be displayed as just the domain. `_@example.com` can therefore appear as `example.com`, but the wire lookup still uses `name=_`.

## Follow the public key, never the address

NIP-05 is not a mutable contact pointer. If a user follows the key returned for `alice@example.com`, the follow list must retain that public key. It must not retain the identifier as an instruction to replace the followed key later.

Suppose the domain maps `alice` to key A today and key B next month. The client should stop showing the NIP-05 identifier for key A once the mapping no longer matches. It must not silently change the existing follow from A to B. A domain transfer, server compromise, configuration error or deliberate reassignment would otherwise rewrite the user’s social graph.

This distinction also matters for Web of Trust calculations. Edges belong to public keys. A current domain mapping can be evidence displayed beside a key, but it is not a substitute node and must not inherit the key’s trust score if the mapping changes.

## Treat the network rules as security rules

The well-known endpoint has several strict requirements:

1. Use HTTPS and the exact domain from the identifier.
2. Ignore redirects. NIP-05 says the endpoint must not return them and fetchers must not follow them.
3. Require lowercase hexadecimal keys and lowercase names.
4. For browser clients, distinguish an invalid mapping from an inconclusive network failure. Missing `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` can make a valid endpoint unreadable to JavaScript.
5. Parse only the requested name from `names`; do not accept a similar spelling or case-folded guess.

These rules prevent a convenient identifier from becoming an open-ended redirect or normalization mechanism. A user-facing status should separate “mapping mismatch” from “could not check,” because they mean different things.

## Relay hints help discovery, not identity

The response may include a recommended `relays` object keyed by public key. Those URLs can help a client find the kind `0` event and other events for the person. They do not strengthen the name-to-key proof, and they do not guarantee that an event exists, was accepted or will remain stored.

Use relay hints as a bounded discovery input. They should not erase the user’s relay configuration or override newer routing information without an explicit policy.

## Cache the result with its time and reason

Checking on every render leaks browsing activity and creates unnecessary load. Caching is reasonable, but a cached badge should not look timeless.

Store at least the identifier, public key, result, checked-at time and failure class. Recheck successful mappings periodically and retry network failures sooner than confirmed mismatches. When a kind `0` event changes its `nip05` field, invalidate the old result immediately.

A practical client state model is:

- **matched**: both directions agree now;
- **mismatched**: the endpoint answered, but the name or key differs;
- **unreachable**: DNS, TLS, HTTP or CORS prevented a conclusive check;
- **invalid**: the identifier, JSON or key format violates NIP-05.

## A safe implementation checklist

Before showing a NIP-05 identifier:

1. Verify the signature of the newest kind `0` event.
2. Validate the identifier syntax and lowercase local part.
3. Fetch the exact well-known URL without following redirects.
4. Compare the exact name to the exact lowercase hex public key.
5. For reverse search, fetch kind `0` and confirm the same identifier there.
6. Keep follows, trust edges and account references anchored to the public key.
7. Record when the check happened and explain inconclusive failures separately.

NIP-05 is useful because it adds human-readable discovery without changing Nostr’s cryptographic identity anchor. The safest interface says exactly what was checked: this domain and this signed key currently agree on this name.

posts.title: Citrine 3.1.1 closes a NIP-42 auth bypass in the Android relay
posts.description: Citrine 3.1.1 verifies the signature on kind 22242 AUTH events before trusting them, scopes subscription ids to their connection, and aligns COUNT, replaceable tie-breaks and OK prefixes with NIP-01 and NIP-45.
posts.excerpt: Citrine checked an AUTH event's kind, challenge, relay tag and timestamp, but never its signature, so a client could authenticate as any pubkey and read the private kinds the relay gates behind NIP-42.

sources.title: Enforce NIP spec conformance across the relay (829f0396)
NIP-42 Authentication of clients to relays

posts.content:
[Citrine 3.1.1](https://github.com/greenart7c3/Citrine/releases/tag/v3.1.1), the relay that runs as an Android app, was published on 11 September 2026. The first entry in its changelog is a security fix, and the rest is a sweep of smaller conformance repairs.

The [comparison against 3.1.0](https://github.com/greenart7c3/Citrine/compare/v3.1.0...v3.1.1) is three commits and eleven files. Almost all of the code arrives in one of them, [829f0396](https://github.com/greenart7c3/Citrine/commit/829f039622efe1e3fae9c3aab2c4e3abd9b639cc), titled "Enforce NIP spec conformance across the relay".

## AUTH without a signature

[NIP-42](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/42.md) lets a relay ask a client to prove which pubkey it controls. The relay sends a challenge string, and the client answers with a signed kind 22242 event carrying that challenge and the relay's URL.

In 3.1.0, `validateAuthEvent` checked that the event was kind 22242, that it carried a challenge and a relay tag, that the challenge matched the one sent on that connection, that the relay URL normalized, and that `created_at` was within ten minutes of the current time. Those are the checks NIP-42 lists. If they passed, the handler added `event.pubKey` to the connection's set of authenticated users.

Nothing in that path verified the signature. The challenge is sent to whoever opens the connection, so a client could build a kind 22242 event with the right challenge, put any pubkey in it, leave the signature invalid, and be treated as that pubkey for the rest of the connection.

Version 3.1.1 adds the missing step after the existing checks:

```kotlin
// NIP-42: an AUTH event must carry a valid signature, otherwise any
// client could authenticate as any pubkey.
if (!event.verify()) {
    connection?.send(CommandResult.invalid(event, "auth event signature verification failed").toJson())
    return
}
```

The commit message names what the authenticated set protected: protected-event writes and private-kind reads. On the read side, `AuthGate` refuses filters for five kinds unless one of the connection's authenticated pubkeys is an author in the filter or appears in its `#p` values. The five include kind 4 direct messages, kind 1059 gift wraps and kind 30078 application data. With a forged AUTH, a client could name the owner's pubkey and pass that gate.

How far that reached depends on configuration. Citrine listens on 127.0.0.1, port 4869, by default, so on a default install the clients that can open a connection are the ones on the same device. The listening address is a setting, and a relay configured to listen elsewhere was open to the same forged AUTH from anything that could reach it. On the write side, the NIP-70 protected-event check already exempted connections from localhost, so the bypass there mattered only for remote connections.

## Subscription ids were global

[NIP-01](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/01.md) says relays must manage subscription ids independently for each WebSocket connection. Citrine kept all subscriptions in one cache keyed by the id the client sent. A `CLOSE` for `"feed"` on one socket cancelled every connection's `"feed"`, and a new `REQ` with the same id replaced it.

The cache key is now the connection name and the id together. The id on the wire is still the one the client chose.

## COUNT is one answer

[NIP-45](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/45.md) says the filters in a `COUNT` are OR'd and aggregated into a single count result. In 3.1.0 a `COUNT` went through the same path as a `REQ`: one count message per filter, then an `EOSE`, and the subscription stayed registered, so it also received live events that matched it later.

Version 3.1.1 gives `COUNT` its own path. It is never registered, so it neither replaces a `REQ` with the same id nor receives live events, and it sends one `COUNT` message with no `EOSE`. The total is the sum of the per-filter counts, so an event that matches two filters in one request is counted twice.

## Smaller repairs

- **The `#p` key.** For filters with no kinds, `AuthGate` looked for receivers under the key `"#p"`, but filter tags are stored without the `#`. An authenticated user asking for `{"#p":[<own pubkey>]}` was refused with `restricted`. The kinds branch already used `"p"`; this one now does too.
- **Replaceable tie-breaks.** NIP-01 says that between replaceable events with the same timestamp, the one with the lowest id is retained. Citrine rejected any incoming event when a stored one had an equal or later `created_at`, so the first to arrive won. Both queries now let an incoming event with an equal timestamp and a lower id replace the stored one.
- **Exact `ids` and `authors`.** The in-memory filter still accepted prefix matches, which the SQL path and NIP-01 do not. Only exact values match now.
- **OK prefixes.** Policy rejections now use `blocked:` rather than `invalid:`, a deleted event gets `deleted:`, and an older replaceable gets `duplicate:`.
- **NIP-11.** The relay information document was built by string interpolation, so a relay name or description containing a quote produced invalid JSON. It is now built with Jackson. NIP-04 is no longer advertised in `supported_nips`, and the CORS headers now include `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`.
- **NIP-86.** `unbanpubkey` and `unallowpubkey` are added, and `allowpubkey` no longer removes a pubkey from the ban list as a side effect.

## What the artifacts establish

Version 3.1.1 is a published release with six Android packages and a signed checksum manifest. The commit message reports `assembleDebug`, `ktlintCheck`, `test` and `lintDebug` passing and 24 behavioral checks run on a device; the diff itself adds no test files. Citrine 3.2.0 followed on 18 September and contains every 3.1.1 commit, so updating to the current release includes the fix. None of this establishes which version a given phone is running, and anyone relying on Citrine for direct messages should check.

posts.title: Amethyst 1.17 stops losing whole requests to one refused kind
posts.description: Amethyst 1.17.0 narrows subscriptions a relay has refused instead of dropping them, reads NIP-92 metadata for profile images and fixes how it checks NIP-49 passwords.
posts.excerpt: One relay closed every request that named a kind it did not serve, so an account's gift wraps, and with them its DMs and White Noise invites, never arrived.

sources.title: PR #4238: drop a kind the relay refuses by name
PR #4239: fit a REQ under a relay's filter-count cap
PR #4320: NIP-92 imeta for profile picture and banner
PR #4209: Backup Keys redesign and NIP-49 fixes

posts.content:
[Amethyst 1.17.0](https://github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/releases/tag/v1.17.0) was published on 5 October 2026 under the title "Cordn and several updates". It is a large release: 1,253 commits since 1.16.0, with 176 pull requests listed in the notes. The release page carries Android packages in F-Droid and Google Play flavors, desktop builds for Linux, macOS and Windows, and separate `amy` and `geode` packages.

Most of those pull requests are refactoring and translations. This article covers four changes a user can actually notice, read from the pull requests and their diffs rather than from the one-line changelog entries.

## A refused kind no longer sinks the whole request

The most consequential fix is about relays that serve only some event kinds. [PR #4238](https://github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/pull/4238) documents a relay running strfry 1.1.1 with a kind allowlist that answers `CLOSED` to any `REQ` whose filter names a kind it does not serve, even when the other kinds in the same filter are fine.

Amethyst asks for gift wraps with a single filter covering kinds `1059` and `21059`. The relay refused `21059`, Amethyst treated the `CLOSED` as a refusal of the entire filter set, and every gift wrap was lost. For an account whose kind `10050` DM relay was that relay, no NIP-17 direct message arrived and neither did any White Noise invite. The Welcome path failed without logging, so nothing pointed at the cause.

The fix teaches the relay pool to read the refusal. When a `CLOSED` reason names a kind, for example `kind not allowed: 21059`, Amethyst records it for that relay and strips the kind from every request it builds for that relay, both on change and on reconnect. A filter left with no kinds at all is dropped rather than sent empty, because an empty kinds list would ask for every kind.

The same relay also closes any request with four or more filters, and it does not advertise a `max_filters` value in its NIP-11 document. Marmot group messages use one filter per group, so an account in four or more groups there loaded no group messages at all. [PR #4239](https://github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/pull/4239), which reached `main` as a re-land in #4242, learns the cap from the refusal: if four filters were refused, the limit is at most three. It then merges filters that differ in exactly one set of values into one filter with the union of those values.

The merge has deliberate limits. Filters with a `limit` are never merged, because a limit per filter and a limit over the union are different requests. Filters that differ in two fields are never merged, because the union would match combinations neither filter asked for. If a request still does not fit, Amethyst sends the first filters up to the cap and logs one warning. The pull request states that some account subscriptions can still be trimmed when a capped relay is the account's only outbox relay, and leaves a full fix for a separate change.

## Profile images follow NIP-92

[PR #4320](https://github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/pull/4320) merged on 5 October, about two hours after NIP-92 began allowing `imeta` tags for kind `0` `picture` and `banner` URLs, a change [reported here earlier today](/news/2026-10-06/nip-92-gives-profile-images-fallbacks-and-blurhashes). A new `ProfileImageMetas` class matches an `imeta` tag to a profile image only when the URLs are equal after trimming whitespace, so a different query string does not match.

Avatars and banners can now show a blurhash placeholder while loading and try the listed fallback URLs if the primary one fails. When a user edits their profile, Amethyst keeps the metadata for an image that did not change and drops it for an image that was replaced or removed. A 291-line test file covers these cases.

## Backup Keys and NIP-49

[PR #4209](https://github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/pull/4209) redesigns the key backup screen. The `nsec` is shown as three numbered rows of uppercase groups, masked until tapped, so it can be copied onto paper. Bech32 is case-insensitive, and login on Android, desktop and `amy` now accepts a key typed back in uppercase with dashes, spaces or line breaks. Before, an uppercase `NSEC1` was rejected.

The password-protected NIP-49 copy now asks for the password twice and requires at least 12 characters when creating a new `ncryptsec`. The diff states that this is a creation policy only, since NIP-49 sets no minimum and decryption must accept passwords other clients allowed.

The same pull request fixes the NIP-49 code itself. Decryption ignored the authentication result and instead treated a decrypted key as wrong if none of its bytes was positive, which rejected a valid key whose 32 bytes all had the high bit set. It now checks the Poly1305 tag. Encryption also ignored its result, so a failure could have produced an `ncryptsec` that no password opens; it now throws. Encrypted payloads that are not exactly 48 bytes are now rejected.

## Cordn arrives

The release title refers to [PR #4201](https://github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/pull/4201), which adds Cordn group messaging: screens for creating, joining and managing groups, and a runtime that handles MLS-encrypted group communication through coordinator servers. It is the largest single change in the release at 51,174 added lines across 419 files. The pull request's test-plan checklist, including its three interop suites, was left unticked.

posts.title: NIP-92 gives profile images fallbacks and blurhashes
posts.description: A merged NIP-92 change lets kind 0 profiles describe pictures and banners with exact-match imeta tags, including fallbacks, dimensions, hashes, blurhashes and alt text.
posts.excerpt: Profile pictures and banners can now carry the same inline media metadata as attachments, without moving their URLs out of the kind 0 profile document.

sources.title: NIP-92: imeta tags for kind 0 picture and banner
NIP-24 Extra metadata fields and tags

posts.content:
[Pull request #2494](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/pull/2494) merged into the Nostr specifications on 5 October 2026. It adds a profile-specific section to [NIP-92](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/92.md): a kind `0` metadata event may now attach `imeta` tags to its `picture` and `banner` URLs.

The patch is small, adding 35 lines to NIP-92 and one cross-reference to [NIP-24](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/24.md), but it closes a practical gap. A note could already describe an attached image with dimensions, a MIME type, a hash, alt text, a blurhash and fallback locations. A profile image could only supply its primary URL inside the JSON string stored in the event's `content` field.

## The URL remains in the profile

The change does not replace the existing kind `0` shape. `picture` remains in the profile JSON, and `banner` remains the optional field recorded by NIP-24. The new data sits in ordinary event tags alongside that content.

An `imeta` tag is associated with a profile field only when its `url` entry is exactly equal to the value of `picture` or `banner`. A shortened URL, a redirected destination or a URL differing only in its query string is not a match. Tags that match neither field should be ignored.

That exact-match rule gives clients a deterministic join between two representations inside one signed event. It also stops a stale tag from being applied to a newly selected image merely because both images came from the same host.

The specification's example gives a profile picture a MIME type, SHA-256 hash, dimensions, blurhash and fallback URL, while the banner carries its MIME type, hash and dimensions. NIP-92 allows any field defined by [NIP-94](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/94.md), so a publisher can also provide `alt`, `size`, thumbnails or other file metadata. Only `url` plus at least one other field is required for an `imeta` tag; the richer fields remain optional.

## A failed host no longer has to mean an empty avatar

The most visible addition is `fallback`. Clients should try declared fallback URLs when the primary profile image fails to load. That can keep an avatar or banner visible through a host outage or a moved file, provided the author published another reachable copy.

The other fields solve different problems. `blurhash` can provide a compact placeholder while the image loads. `dim` lets a layout reserve the correct aspect ratio before downloading the file. `alt` gives clients an accessibility description. The `x` field can carry the file's SHA-256 hash, although NIP-92 does not require it and clients still have to verify it for the hash to provide an integrity check.

These are hints carried by the profile author, not a storage layer. The merge does not upload a mirror, prove that a fallback will stay online or force a client to use any field. The normative language is mostly `MAY` and `SHOULD`, so a profile still needs a usable primary URL and compatibility still depends on client implementations.

## Replaceable events create a maintenance rule

Kind `0` is replaceable: a newer event from the same public key supersedes the older profile. That makes metadata preservation part of the publishing path.

The new section says a client publishing a new kind `0` should carry over the `imeta` tags for a picture or banner that has not changed and drop tags for images no longer in use. Without that rule, editing a display name in a client that understands profile media metadata could accidentally erase fallbacks and alt text. Carrying every old tag forward would be worse, because it would leave signed metadata for images the profile no longer references.

Clients that do not implement the addition can continue reading `picture` and `banner` exactly as before. They may ignore the new tags, which makes the format backward compatible. The tradeoff is a mixed deployment period: one client may show a fallback or blurhash while another shows a broken primary image.

## What changed, and what did not

The merged text establishes a common format for describing profile media. It does not certify media hosts, move profiles to content-addressed storage or make a hash mandatory. It also does not retroactively enrich existing profiles. New tags appear only when a user or client publishes a new kind `0` event containing them.

The pull request says Ditto and Armada already implement the shape, but that statement comes from the submitter and the specification does not maintain a compatibility registry. Other clients need to adopt both the publishing and rendering sides before the metadata travels reliably across the ecosystem.

For implementers, the safe sequence is narrow: keep the canonical URL in the profile JSON, emit at most one matching `imeta` tag per image, compare URLs exactly, preserve tags only for unchanged fields, and treat every fallback as untrusted network input. The result is incremental rather than dramatic, but it gives profile images the same recovery and presentation vocabulary that Nostr attachments already had.

posts.title: Nostream 3.2.0 adds blue/green relay updates and actionable moderation
posts.description: Nostream 3.2.0 adds an optional HAProxy blue/green stack, default-off NIP-56 hiding and fixes for quiet multi-filter query failures.
posts.excerpt: Relay operators gain a rolling two-process topology and an opt-in way to act on trusted reports, with important validation and policy limits.
posts.content:
[Nostream 3.2.0](https://github.com/cameri/nostream/releases/tag/v3.2.0) gives relay operators two new decisions to make. One is operational: whether to run two relay processes behind HAProxy and replace them one at a time. The other is editorial: whether reports from configured trusted moderators should hide events from relay queries. The same release also fixes query shapes that could silently omit events.

This is a published source release, not a new project launch. Nostream has existed since 2022 and is already indexed in the ecosystem directory. Version 3.2.0 was published on 3 October 2026, inside this watch window.

## An optional blue/green relay topology

[Pull request #777](https://github.com/cameri/nostream/pull/777) adds an alternative Docker Compose stack with two relay containers, named blue and green, behind HAProxy. HAProxy checks each relay through the unauthenticated /readyz endpoint. If a backend stops being ready, option redispatch lets HAProxy retry an eligible failed request against the other backend.

A rolling script replaces one relay, waits for its replacement to report healthy, then moves to the second. The stack also enables a Redis stream fan-out so live events accepted by either relay can reach WebSocket clients connected to both processes. The existing single-relay deployment remains available. Operators opt into the new topology by using the separate compose file.

The release calls this a zero-downtime update path, but the underlying PR records a narrower validation result. Its author checked the Compose configuration and HAProxy syntax, then stated that the rolling script had not yet been exercised against a live stack with a WebSocket client connected. The implementation is therefore a documented deployment option, not independent proof that every cutover will preserve every connection.

## Reports can now affect query results

[Pull request #788](https://github.com/cameri/nostream/pull/788) adds the setting nip56.hideActionableReports. It is false by default and only has an effect when NIP-56 handling is also enabled.

When both settings are active, a report from a configured trusted moderator can become actionable. An event-targeted report hides that event from REQ and COUNT results. A pubkey-targeted report hides events authored by that pubkey. Before this change, Nostream could record that a report was actionable without changing what subscribers received.

This remains an operator policy choice. [NIP-56](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/56.md) describes kind 1984 reports as subjective signals and warns that automatic relay moderation can be gamed. Version 3.2.0 does not decide which reports are correct, does not enable hiding by default, and does not remove the underlying event from other relays.

## Quiet query failures get explicit fixes

[Pull request #792](https://github.com/cameri/nostream/pull/792) addresses two query bugs. A filter with more than one tag name previously tried to satisfy all tag conditions from one joined database row, so a valid event could fail to match. Nostream now uses a separate EXISTS subquery for each tag name.

The same patch wraps each filter before combining several filters with UNION. That keeps a limit on the first filter from capping the entire request and prevents it from breaking COUNT queries. The release also changes nostream info and nostream invite create so they fail instead of hanging indefinitely when the database cannot be reached.

These changes matter because the failures were quiet. A client could receive end-of-stored-events with no matching events and no obvious server error. The release provides unit-level and configuration evidence for the fixes, but this review did not operate a production relay or reproduce traffic under load.

For operators, 3.2.0 is best read as a set of controls with explicit boundaries: an optional deployment topology, an opt-in moderation action and corrected query behavior. Adoption, live cutover behavior and moderation policy still depend on each relay operator.

posts.title: Amber 6.6.7 gives dead relays a second chance after fifteen minutes
posts.description: Amber 6.6.7 makes a relay's dead state expire after a 15 minute cooldown, stops counting each failed dial twice, and rebuilds relay sockets when a VPN comes up or the device regains internet access.
posts.excerpt: A relay marked dead stayed dead until the app was force closed, and because a failed dial was recorded twice it took five attempts rather than ten to get there.
posts.content:
[Amber 6.6.7](https://github.com/greenart7c3/Amber/releases/tag/v6.6.7) was published on 5 October 2026. Eight commits and twenty three files separate it from 6.6.6, and the bulk of the change is in how the signer decides a relay is no longer worth dialling.

The reported symptom was that relays stayed disconnected until the app was force closed. The [comparison against 6.6.6](https://github.com/greenart7c3/Amber/compare/v6.6.6...v6.6.7) shows two independent causes, both in the retry accounting rather than in the sockets themselves.

## Dead was permanent

`RelayHealthTracker` keeps a streak of consecutive connection failures per relay and stops retrying once the streak passes `MAX_RECONNECT_ATTEMPTS`, which is 10. A dead relay is also dropped from the subscription relay set, so the periodic refresh stops opening sockets to it.

In 6.6.6 that state was cleared only by a successful connection, an operating system network change, or a manual reconnect. The tracker stored a bare failure count, and `isDead` was a comparison against that count alone. Nothing expired it.

That is survivable when every outage arrives as a network change, and it is not what happens. The new documentation in the file names the cases it misses: a Wi-Fi network that lost internet access and got it back, a weak cell signal, a relay outage. None of those is a change of default network, so none of them reset the tracker, and every relay could be marked dead while the device stayed on one apparently healthy network.

Version 6.6.7 stores a timestamp alongside the count and makes the dead state expire:

```kotlin
const val DEAD_COOLDOWN_MS = 15 * 60 * 1000L

fun isDead(relay: NormalizedRelayUrl): Boolean {
    val entry = health[relay] ?: return false
    return entry.failures > MAX_RECONNECT_ATTEMPTS && clock() - entry.lastFailureAt < DEAD_COOLDOWN_MS
}
```

Fifteen minutes after its last failure a relay is eligible again and the periodic refresh re-adds it. The threshold is unchanged; what changed is that exceeding it is now a timed penalty rather than a verdict. A clock function is injected so the expiry can be tested without waiting.

## Each failed dial was counted twice

The second cause is narrower and sharper. Quartz, the library driving the relay pool, reports a failed dial as `onCannotConnect` followed by `onDisconnected`. Both handlers called the same `scheduleReconnect`, which recorded a failure.

So the streak advanced by two per failed dial. The documented threshold of 10 was reached after five. The comment added in 6.6.7 states both halves of the problem: counting both callbacks halved the real threshold, and a plain server-side close is not a connection failure at all.

The repair splits the one function in two. `recordFailureAndScheduleReconnect` records a failure and is called only from `onCannotConnect`. `scheduleReconnect` now checks `isDead` and reconnects without recording anything, which is what `onDisconnected` needs.

## Network changes that were not a change of network

The release also rebuilds relay connections when a VPN comes up or goes down, and when the device regains internet access, rather than only when it switches between Wi-Fi and mobile data.

A new file, `NetworkChangeDetector.kt`, holds that decision in 79 lines with no Android service dependencies. It reduces the default network to a snapshot of three fields: the network handle, the set of reported transports, and whether Android validated that the network actually reaches the internet. Comparing successive snapshots, it reports a reset is needed when the handle changes, when the transport set changes, when an unvalidated network becomes validated, or when a network returns after being lost.

Two of those are the VPN cases. A VPN network reports its own `TRANSPORT_VPN` and its underlying transport, so a VPN taking over as the default network changes the handle, and a VPN moving from Wi-Fi to mobile changes the transport set while the default network stays the same. The detector distinguishes the two directions and labels them, so the reset carries a reason.

It is equally explicit about what is not a change. The first callback after registering is the network the relays are already connecting on, so it is recorded as a baseline and reports nothing. Repeated callbacks for the same state report nothing. Losing a network that had already been replaced reports nothing.

`ConnectivityService` was reworked around it, losing 46 lines and gaining 81. Both `onAvailable` and `onCapabilitiesChanged` now feed one `onNetworkState` function. Resets are debounced by `NETWORK_SETTLE_MS`, one second, because the callbacks arrive in bursts as validation completes and the relays should be rebuilt once, on the final network. Capabilities are tracked even while the kill switch is on, so the baseline is current when relays are allowed back.

## Requests from browsers that are not Chrome

A separate entry restores compatibility with web clients. A `nostrsigner:` request can carry its parameters either in intent extras, which is what [NIP-55](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/55.md) describes for native Android callers, or in the URI query string, which is what a web page does. Amber decided between them by looking for a single extra, `Browser.EXTRA_APPLICATION_ID`.

Chrome sets it. Other browsers do not. DuckDuckGo is named in the changelog, and a request from it took the native path and failed with "Unknown signer type".

The new `isWebRequest` accepts three weaker signals in addition to that extra: the `BROWSABLE` intent category, a referrer that resolves to a browser, and a `type=` parameter in the query string, checked both raw and percent decoded. A `type` extra still takes precedence, since it means the caller used the extras API and is native. Resolving a referrer to a browser needs package visibility, so `AndroidManifest.xml` adds a `<queries>` entry for `VIEW` plus `BROWSABLE` on `https`.

## A foreign key that IGNORE did not cover

The last entry fixes a crash when a permission was saved for an application that had just been deleted or reset. `insertPermissions2` was annotated `OnConflictStrategy.IGNORE`, which covers uniqueness conflicts and not foreign key failures, so the insert raised `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_FOREIGNKEY`. It now reads the surviving application keys first and drops permissions whose parent is gone, and `insertPermissions` was routed through it instead of calling the raw insert directly.

## What the artifacts establish

Version 6.6.7 is a published release tagged at commit `dc3f672e`, with eleven Android packages and a signed checksum manifest. Nineteen test cases arrive with it: four on the cooldown, eight on the change detector, and seven on the web request decision. The changelog and the diff agree on all four entries.

That establishes what the code does. It does not establish that any device is running it, and store and repository channels move at their own pace. Someone whose signer kept losing its relays should check the version actually installed.

posts.title: nak 0.21.0 reads relay lists and resolves petname paths
posts.description: nak 0.21.0 adds a relays command that prints a pubkey's NIP-65 relays with inbox and outbox filters, and teaches every pubkey argument to resolve NIP-02 petname paths. Seventeen commits separate it from 0.20.7.
posts.excerpt: The release notes are empty, so the diff is the only account of it. Two additions stand out: a new subcommand for NIP-65 relay lists, and petname path resolution wired into the shared pubkey parser rather than into one command.

sources.title: Pull request #220: Resolve relative petnames using the selected signer
Correct nak event behaviour if 0 lines received from an open stdin

posts.content:
[nak](https://github.com/fiatjaf/nak), the Nostr command-line tool, tagged [v0.21.0](https://github.com/fiatjaf/nak/releases/tag/v0.21.0) on 3 October 2026. The release body is empty, so the [seventeen commits since v0.20.7](https://github.com/fiatjaf/nak/compare/v0.20.7...v0.21.0) are the only account of what changed. Two of them add capabilities rather than fix behaviour, and both land on specifications this site has covered before.

## A command for NIP-65 relay lists

[`55707c26`](https://github.com/fiatjaf/nak/commit/55707c26af51b0c10611b962037a6d833ecd4778) adds `relays.go`, a 58 line file registering a new top-level subcommand. Its usage string states the scope: `prints the nip65 relays for a given pubkey, one relay per line`.

It takes a pubkey as an argument or on standard input and writes one relay URL per line. Two flags narrow the output, each aliased to the other half of the NIP-65 vocabulary:

```
--inbox, --read     only print relays marked as inbox/read
--outbox, --write   only print relays marked as outbox/write
```

The filter logic is worth reading literally, because the combined case is not a union. Passing both flags requires both marks on the same relay:

```go
if wantInbox && wantOutbox {
    if !(rl.Inbox && rl.Outbox) {
        continue
    }
}
```

So `--inbox --outbox` prints only the relays serving both directions, which under NIP-65 is what an unmarked `r` tag produces, while passing neither prints the whole list. The two flags together narrow the set rather than widening it, which matters when the output feeds a publish step.

The direction names map onto the roles described in [the NIP-65 routing guide published earlier today](/news/2026-10-04/use-nip-65-relay-lists-without-losing-posts-or-mentions): an author's outbox relays are where their events are fetched from, and a recipient's inbox relays are where events mentioning them are delivered. The command makes both targets scriptable without parsing a kind 10002 event by hand.

## Petname paths, in the shared parser

NIP-02 petname paths arrive in two stages, and the second corrects the first. This is the feature added to NIP-02 in the revision reported on [20 September](/news/2026-09-20/nip-02-gives-petnames-resolvable-paths), and constrained to ASCII in [the follow-up three days later](/news/2026-09-23/nip-02-limits-petnames-to-ascii).

[`4011cba5`](https://github.com/fiatjaf/nak/commit/4011cba5c56c03ee8b9d03fcc2dc3215836e7108) does not add a command. It changes the shared parser: `parsePubKey` takes a second argument, a pubkey to resolve from, and dispatches anything beginning with a tilde to a new `resolvePetnamePath`.

```go
func parsePubKey(value string, from nostr.PubKey) (nostr.PubKey, error) {
	value = strings.TrimPrefix(value, "nostr:")

	if strings.HasPrefix(value, "~") {
		return resolvePetnamePath(value, from)
	}
```

That helper calls `sys.ResolvePetnamePath` under a five second timeout. Its doc comment states the mechanism and gives the mixed form NIP-02 allows: the path `~erin/david/frank` walks the follow list of each name in the chain, and the first name may instead be a NIP-05 identifier, as in `~erin@names.com/david/frank`. Because the underlying profile lookup hides NIP-05 errors, a failed resolution is re-checked against `nip05.QueryIdentifier`, so a DNS or HTTP problem is reported as itself rather than as an unresolvable petname. The commit updates every call site and adds 239 lines of tests.

What that stage did not settle is which key a relative path starts from. [Pull request #220](https://github.com/fiatjaf/nak/pull/220), merged on 25 September, adds `petname_cli.go` and a `parsePubKeyForCommand` wrapper that classifies the root:

```go
absolute := hexErr == nil || nip05.IsValidIdentifier(parts[0]) ||
    (nip19Err == nil && (prefix == "npub" || prefix == "nprofile"))
```

A path rooted in a hex pubkey, a valid NIP-05 identifier, or an `npub` or `nprofile` is absolute, and a comment records why the case is separated: `Absolute roots must also work without access to a signing key.` Only a relative path calls `gatherKeyerFromArguments` and takes that signer's public key as the starting point. Reading outward from someone you can name therefore needs no key, while a path starting from your own follows does.

The same pull request fixes an argument-order problem. An `init` call applies `deferPetnameFlags` across the whole command tree, replacing every pubkey-carrying flag with a wrapper that stores the raw string and resolves it only once all flags are parsed. The comment gives the reason: a signer flag such as `--sec` may appear after the petname flag on the command line, and the resolution needs the signer. It adds 169 further lines of tests.

## Completions, and three smaller corrections

[`5f28b21c`](https://github.com/fiatjaf/nak/commit/5f28b21cbde99d0066c15c9ba31d8e4dd6ca0e49) sets `EnableShellCompletion: true` on the root command, exposing `nak completion bash`, `zsh` and `fish`. The README gains the three install paths for shells whose package does not wire this up.

Three behaviour fixes are narrow, but each closes a case where the tool did something unhelpful instead of reporting a problem:

- [`30551476`](https://github.com/fiatjaf/nak/commit/30551476c533c31591c5c3b5de6ff85fb722a167) adds `--github` to `nak event`, whose usage line gives the reason: `treat empty stdin as no stdin at all, as GitHub Actions always opens it`. In that environment an always-open but empty standard input was indistinguishable from piped input.
- `nak key encrypt` given a single argument now fails with `no password given or key piped on stdin` when standard input is not a pipe, instead of reading the lone argument as a password with no key to apply it to.
- `blossom` drops `Required: true` from its `--server` flag, so a server can be given per subcommand, and a missing one now produces `no server specified`. `blossom upload` gains `--auto`, which resolves the current user's advertised media servers instead. `nsite download` accepts an `nevent1` or `naddr1` pointer as well as a site URL, fetching from the author's write relays and any hints the pointer carries.

## What it means in practice

Both additions remove a hand-rolled step for anyone scripting against Nostr. Answering where to publish or where to read no longer means fetching and parsing a kind 10002 event, and a follow path can be written where a 64 character hex string used to go. Neither changes any specification: this is a tool catching up to NIP-02 and NIP-65 as they already stand. The absolute-root rule is the detail to carry away, because a petname path starting from your own follows will ask for a key.

posts.title: Use NIP-65 relay lists without losing posts or mentions
posts.description: NIP-65 separates relays used to publish a person's events from relays used to receive mentions. The direction changes where clients should look.
posts.excerpt: A NIP-65 relay list is directional. Write relays are where a person publishes; read relays are where other people should deliver events that mention them.
posts.seoDescription: Learn how NIP-65 kind 10002 relay lists use read and write markers, how clients route posts and mentions, and how to avoid common relay-list mistakes.

sources.title: NIP-65: Relay List Metadata at commit 0046368
NIP-01: Basic protocol flow at commit 0046368

posts.content:
A Nostr client cannot assume that every relay serves the same role. A person may publish their own events to one set of relays and watch another set for events that mention them. [NIP-65](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/0046368a747c5c25ae2bec28bae0e537744c8f10/65.md) gives clients a signed way to advertise that split with a replaceable kind `10002` event.

The direction is easy to reverse by mistake. A person's **write** relays are where their events can be found. Their **read** relays are where other authors should send events that tag them. Getting this wrong can make a healthy relay setup look like lost posts or missing mentions.

## Read and write describe the list owner's behavior

A kind `10002` event stores relay URLs in `r` tags. The optional third value is `read` or `write`:

```json
{
  "kind": 10002,
  "tags": [
    ["r", "wss://posts.example", "write"],
    ["r", "wss://mentions.example", "read"],
    ["r", "wss://both.example"]
  ],
  "content": ""
}
```

The unmarked relay belongs to both groups. These labels are from the list owner's point of view. `write` means "I generally publish my events here." `read` means "I generally read mentions here." They are not permissions and do not promise that a relay will accept a connection, store an event or keep it indefinitely.

Because kind `10002` is in NIP-01's replaceable range, the newest event for a public key supersedes older versions. A client editing the list should publish a complete replacement, not a partial patch. If two versions have the same timestamp, NIP-01 says the event with the lowest ID wins lexically.

## Finding a person's posts uses their write relays

To download events **from** a person, NIP-65 says clients should query that person's write relays. This includes their ordinary notes and other events they authored.

That may sound backward if "write" is read as an instruction for the current client. It is not. It records where the list owner writes, so it tells everyone else where to read that owner's output.

If a profile appears empty in one client, inspect the profile's kind `10002` event before concluding that the posts are gone. The client may know the public key but be searching only its own default relays. Adding the author's advertised write relays to the fetch plan can restore discovery without changing the user's permanent relay configuration.

## Delivering a mention uses the recipient's read relays

When publishing an event, a client should send it to the author's write relays. If the event tags another person, it should also send the event to that person's read relays. This is the other half of the route: author storage plus recipient delivery.

Suppose Alice writes on Relay A and reads mentions on Relay B. Bob's client should publish Bob's reply to Bob's own write relays and to Alice's Relay B. Looking only at Alice's Relay A may find her posts, but it does not follow her declared inbox route.

This does not guarantee delivery. A relay may require authentication, payment or another policy check. The recipient may change their list, and clients may implement NIP-65 differently. The relay list is routing metadata, not a receipt.

## Keep the list small and make it discoverable

NIP-65 recommends two to four relays in each category. A long list multiplies connections, duplicate events and publication work. More relays can improve redundancy, but every additional destination has a cost and may expose more of a user's activity pattern.

The relay-list event itself also has to be found. NIP-65 tells clients to spread it broadly, including to well-known public indexers that other clients use to discover relay lists. It should also accompany the events published to the selected relays. Otherwise a perfectly formed list can remain invisible to the clients that need it.

## A practical check sequence

When posts or mentions appear missing:

1. Fetch the newest valid kind `10002` event for the public key.
2. Treat unmarked `r` tags as both read and write.
3. Query the person's write relays for events they authored.
4. Publish tagged events to the recipient's read relays as well as the author's write relays.
5. Record relay acceptance separately from the routing choice.
6. Fall back carefully when no list is discoverable, because absence of a list is not proof that any particular default is correct.

NIP-65 does not create one global relay set. It lets each person publish directions for two different flows. Following those directions makes relay behavior easier to debug and reduces the chance that a client mistakes a routing mismatch for missing data.

posts.title: Nostr WoT 0.8.10 isolates nonstandard login approvals
posts.description: The extension keeps a narrow compatibility path for one nonstandard login format, but requires a warning and a fresh decision for every request.
posts.excerpt: Version 0.8.10 lets an explicitly supported legacy login continue without turning it into a reusable permission. Every request stays separate.
posts.seoDescription: See how Nostr WoT 0.8.10 handles legacy kind 22242 website logins, why NIP-98 kind 27235 binds more request details, and what remains unverified.
posts.content:
[Nostr WoT extension 0.8.10](https://github.com/nostr-wot/nostr-wot-extension/releases/tag/v0.8.10) keeps website login working for an explicitly supported client that sends a nonstandard authentication event.
